idiom_name: std::shared_ptr body + detach-on-write (COW handle); the control block count is atomic
implementation_notes: The classic C++ realization wraps the payload in a std::shared_ptr and detaches on non-const access: copying a handle increments the reference count (cheap, shared body) and the first mutating operation clones the body when it is not uniquely owned (use_count() != 1; unique() is deprecated in C++20, so compare use_count()). The thread-safe half is provided at the count level - cppreference: 'the control block of a shared_ptr is thread-safe: different non-atomic shared_ptr objects can be accessed using mutable operations ... simultaneously by multiple threads, even when these instances are copies' - which is exactly the row's 'with the reference count protected'. That guarantee does not cover the same shared_ptr object: a handle replaced by a writer while a reader loads it is a data race unless the handle is an std::atomic<std::shared_ptr>, which is what the second variant is for. Keep this form when each thread owns its own handle and only the counts are shared; note also that the standard-library containers no longer take the COW route (C++11 'forbids Copy-On-Write strings', so libstdc++ replaced its COW std::string in GCC 5.1) - the idiom now lives in your own types.
pitfalls: The count is protected, the handle is not: reading a shared_ptr that another thread assigns without synchronisation is a data race, so a swappable handle must be an std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> (C++20) or use the atomic_load/atomic_store free functions.

Returning an interior non-const reference defeats copy-on-write: if operator[] hands out char&, the write happens through the shared body - the unshareable-flag failure documented by the More C++ Idioms page from Sutter's Items 13-16 - so detach on every non-const access or forbid interior references.

use_count()/unique() as a policy test is racy: between the test and the clone another thread may take a reference, and unique() is deprecated since C++20 - make the decision inside the handle's own synchronisation, or accept that uniqueness is only a hint.
sources: More C++ Idioms (Wikibooks), Copy-on-write - the generic CowPtr with detach() and the unshareable-flag pitfall: https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/More_C%2B%2B_Idioms/Copy-on-write

cppreference, std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> - control-block thread safety for distinct shared_ptr objects, and the data race on unsynchronized access to the same shared_ptr: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/memory/shared_ptr/atomic2
GCC libstdc++ manual, Dual ABI - why the library replaced its COW std::string (C++11 forbids Copy-On-Write strings): https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/libstdc++/manual/using_dual_abi.html

variants.name: Atomically published snapshot (mutex-serialized writers)
variants.idiom_name: std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> snapshot swap (C++11 fallback: the atomic_load/atomic_store free functions)
variants.implementation_notes: Readers load the current body with one atomic operation and work on it off the snapshot, while writers serialise on a mutex, clone the loaded snapshot, apply the change and store the new shared_ptr - which drops the old body when its last reader releases it. C++20 provides this directly through std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>; C++11 has the (deprecated in C++20) std::atomic_load/atomic_store free functions. This is the realization the More C++ Idioms Thread-safe Copy-on-write page describes. The reader path is only notionally lock-free: std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> is not required to be lock-free, which is why that page reaches for folly::atomic_shared_ptr - call is_lock_free() when the guarantee matters.
pitfalls: Assume lock-free and you may get a mutex inside the atomic: std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> implementations commonly use a lock, so a reader that takes the load in a hot path should verify is_lock_free() (or use a library that guarantees it).
The snapshot must be deep-const: Config's members are shared with every reader, so a mutable member reached through the const snapshot breaks the guarantee the swap was supposed to provide.
Writers that forget the mutex lose updates silently: load, clone and store is not atomic as a whole, so two writers must share the lock (or a compare_exchange retry loop).
sources: More C++ Idioms (Wikibooks), Thread-safe Copy-on-write - the atomic snapshot with a mutex-serialized update and the folly::atomic_shared_ptr note: https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/More_C%2B%2B_Idioms/Thread-safe_Copy-on-write
cppreference, std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> - load/store/CAS semantics and use_count guarantees for the atomic specialization: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/memory/shared_ptr/atomic2
